title: A Parable, a Prediction, and a Request

verses.text: "For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.
He agreed to pay them a denarius for the day and sent them into his vineyard.
About the third hour he went out and saw others standing in the marketplace doing nothing.
'You also go into my vineyard,' he said, 'and I will pay you whatever is right.'
So they went. He went out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour and did the same thing.
About the eleventh hour he went out and found still others standing around. 'Why have you been standing here all day long doing nothing?' he asked.
'Because no one has hired us,' they answered. So he told them, 'You also go into my vineyard.'
When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, 'Call the workers and pay them their wages, starting with the last ones hired and moving on to the first.'
The workers who were hired about the eleventh hour came and each received a denarius.
So when the original workers came, they assumed they would receive more. But each of them also received a denarius.
On receiving their pay, they began to grumble against the landowner.
'These men who were hired last worked only one hour,' they said, 'and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden and the scorching heat of the day.'
But he answered one of them, 'Friend, I am not being unfair to you. Did you not agree with me on one denarius?
Take your pay and go. I want to give this last man the same as I gave you.
Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine? Or are you envious because I am generous?'
So the last will be first, and the first will be last."
As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, He took the twelve disciples aside and said,
"Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death
and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified. And on the third day He will be raised to life."
Then the mother of Zebedee's sons came to Jesus with her sons and knelt down to make a request of Him.
"What do you want?" He inquired. She answered, "Declare that in Your kingdom one of these two sons of mine may sit at Your right hand, and the other at Your left."
"You do not know what you are asking," Jesus replied. "Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?" "We can," the brothers answered.
"You will indeed drink My cup," Jesus said. "But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom My Father has prepared them."
When the ten heard about this, they were indignant with the two brothers.
But Jesus called them aside and said, "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them.
It shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant,
and whoever wants to be first among you must be your slave —
just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many."
As they were leaving Jericho, a large crowd followed Him.
And there were two blind men sitting beside the road. When they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, "Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!"
The crowd admonished them to be silent, but they cried out all the louder, "Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!"
Jesus stopped and called them. "What do you want Me to do for you?" He asked.
"Lord," they answered, "let our eyes be opened."
Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes, and at once they received their sight and followed Him.

context.author: Matthew, writing to a Jewish audience
context.genre: Parable followed by narrative — a teaching on kingdom generosity, the third and most detailed passion prediction, a family's request, and a healing.
context.audience: Jewish-Christian readers, watching Jesus deliberately overturn expectations about reward, status, and greatness as He nears Jerusalem.
context.setting: Day laborers in this era gathered in village marketplaces before dawn hoping to be hired for the day — a standard workday ran roughly 6am to 6pm, and any day without work meant no food. Jesus' landowner returning four separate times (9am, noon, 3pm, 5pm) to keep hiring reflects unusual, deliberate generosity.
context.custom: A denarius (v.2) was the standard daily wage for unskilled labor — Roman coins bearing Tiberius Caesar's image from this exact period have been recovered by archaeologists, confirming the coin's use and value.
context.timelineImmediate: This chapter sits between Peter's question about reward (closing chapter 19) and the Triumphal Entry (opening chapter 21) — the parable directly answers Peter, while the third passion prediction (v.17-19) is Jesus' most explicit yet, naming crucifixion specifically for the first time.
context.timelineBible: "A ransom for many" (v.28) draws on Exodus 30:12-16, where silver ransomed a life, and anticipates Isaiah 53:11-12's suffering servant who bears the guilt of "many" — language the earliest church (1 Timothy 2:5-6, 1 Peter 1:18-19) read directly back onto Jesus.

translation.meaning: Literally "good" — the landowner's question is really "is your eye evil because mine is good," contrasting envy with generosity as opposite postures of the heart.
A common image for one's appointed portion or fate — here specifically Jesus' coming suffering, which He says James and John will indeed share.
Two escalating terms for lowly service — Jesus moves from the more general "servant" to the starker "slave" to make His point about greatness unmistakable.

occurrences.note: Figure given is for "doulos" (slave), the starker of the two terms — "diakonos" (servant), the milder word, has its own separate, smaller count.

translation.meaning: The price paid to free a slave or captive — Jesus applies this economic/legal term directly to His own coming death.

occurrences.note: Used only twice in the whole New Testament — here and in Mark's parallel account of this same saying — and both times on Jesus' own lips about His own death.

gospelParallels.note: Mark's parallel account of the third passion prediction and the request from James and John themselves (rather than through their mother).
Luke's version of the passion prediction and the healing near Jericho, describing one blind man rather than two.

otBackground.note: The vineyard as an image for God's people, background for the parable's central setting.
The concept of a ransom price paid for a life, echoed directly in v.28.
The suffering servant bearing the guilt of "many" — closely echoed in Jesus' description of His own coming death.

context.sparkNotes: A landowner pays every vineyard worker the same wage regardless of hours worked, illustrating God's generosity. Jesus then predicts His death a third time using the word "ransom" — used only twice in the whole New Testament — directly echoing Isaiah 53:11-12's suffering servant who bears the guilt of many.

commentary.note: Henry reads the parable's core point as a correction, not a contradiction: the reward for a life of service isn't wages earned by the hour, but a gift given by grace — "not as wages for the value of their work, but as the gift of God." To the grumbling laborer, the master's answer is simple: you received exactly what you agreed to; his generosity elsewhere took nothing from you.

Spurgeon notes the emotional turn in the early workers' reaction: they had exactly what was promised, a fair wage, freely agreed to — yet "as soon as the penny was in their hand, a murmur was in their mouth." Their only real grievance, he observes dryly, was that the master had been too generous to those who worked less.

Wesley works out the actual value of a day's wage for his own 18th-century readers: the Roman penny (denarius) equaled roughly fourteen cents in his era's money — a modest but real sum, making the landowner's generosity to the last-hired workers genuinely costly, not merely symbolic.
